clue.text: One released by popular request from pub band and soprano

parts.note: a bar is a pub or the counter in one
Abba was the Swedish pop group
S is the standard abbreviation for soprano in music

explanation.surface: A soprano and a band booked into a pub are let go after public demand.
explanation.walkthrough: The crowd in the Gospels chose to have the robber freed instead of Jesus, hence 'by popular request'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Gospels Pilate let the crowd choose a prisoner to free, and they picked this thief over Jesus.

clue.text: "Or is 't a Norman whose victorious hand / With English blood — thy conquered Land?" (Anne Bradstreet)

definitions.text: "Or is 't a Norman whose victorious hand / With English blood — thy conquered Land?" (Anne Bradstreet)

parts.words: "Or is 't a Norman whose victorious hand / With English blood — thy conquered Land?" (Anne Bradstreet)
parts.note: a quotation clue: the missing word in Bradstreet's line about the Norman conquest is the verb meaning wets with drops, as blood soaking the land

explanation.surface: A line of Anne Bradstreet's verse with one word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: Quotation clues are a TLS staple: the blank is filled by the word the poet used, and the count plus the sense (blood wetting the ground) point to it.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means moistens with drops, as dew does grass, here used of blood soaking conquered ground.

clue.text: New Orleans misanthrope seriously making one irate primarily

indicators.note: making one thing into another signals that one letter in the word is swapped for a new one

parts.note: really, as in 'are you seriously asking', means seriously
a, the indefinite article, means one

indicators.note: primarily means the first letter of the word irate is taken

explanation.surface: Someone sour in New Orleans is truly managing to make a person angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making one irate primarily' turns the A (one) of REALLY into I, the first letter of 'irate'. Ignatius J. Reilly is the grumbling hero of John Kennedy Toole's novel A Confederacy of Dunces, set in New Orleans.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignatius J. Reilly, the scornful anti-hero of A Confederacy of Dunces, rails against everyone in his New Orleans home.

clue.text: People like 17 hits cut by non-spaced out Adam Ant!

indicators.note: something cut by another piece is split open with that piece placed in the gap

parts.note: blows are hits or punches
the singer's name written with no space becomes adamant, and adamant means hard or unyielding

explanation.surface: A pop star's hits get edited by someone who disapproves of his spaced-out persona.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut by' signals the container. Closing the gap in 'Adam Ant' (a 1980s British pop singer) gives 'adamant'. 17 refers to Shakespeare's famous braggart knight.
explanation.definitionFit: Falstaff is the great boaster of Shakespeare, so braggarts and windbags are people of his kind.

clue.text: Man who wrote acts is rather ill, having got drunk with rum

indicators.note: having got drunk suggests the letters are reeling into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A playwright feels poorly after a session on the rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got drunk' scrambles the letters of RATHER ILL and RUM. The playwright wrote Death of a Salesman; 'acts' hints at stage plays.
explanation.definitionFit: The American dramatist wrote plays divided into acts, such as The Crucible and Death of a Salesman.

clue.text: Life-extending drug given to son invigorates

parts.note: in Frank Herbert's Dune the drug melange, called the spice, prolongs life
S is the usual abbreviation for son in family trees

explanation.surface: A youngster is given an elixir of long life and feels revived.
explanation.walkthrough: The life-extending spice is the drug at the centre of the novel Dune. As a verb, to spice up is to liven up, so the definition is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To liven something up is to add flavour or zest to it, so the verb means enlivens.

clue.text: Way to get around foremost of linesmen or a lineswoman

indicators.note: a word made to get around another piece encloses it, so the path wraps round the letter

parts.note: a path is a way or track

indicators.note: foremost of means the first letter of the word linesmen is used

explanation.surface: A football official, or a woman doing the same job, finds a route round the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get around' puts L, the first letter of 'linesmen', inside PATH. The poet is a 'lineswoman' because she wrote lines of verse, not because she ran a touchline.
explanation.definitionFit: Sylvia Plath was a poet, and a poet is a writer of lines of verse, so she is jokingly a woman of lines.

clue.text: Electra complex possessing one French theatre director

indicators.note: possessing means holding something within, so one piece sits inside the other
complex means intricately tangled, so the letters of the name are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A psychoanalytic term for a daughter's fixation seems to have taken hold of a French stage figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complex' rearranges ELECTRA and 'possessing' puts I inside. Jules Claretie ran the Comédie-Française for many years; 'Electra complex' makes the anagram signal look like Freudian jargon.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Claretie was administrator of the Comédie-Française, the national theatre of France, from 1885 to 1913.

clue.text: Sort of news Quoyle covers drinking around hotel

indicators.note: around means the drinking word goes round the letter for hotel

parts.note: sipping means drinking in small mouthfuls
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A journalist type is having a drink in the area of a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' places H inside SIPPING. Quoyle is the reporter in Annie Proulx's novel The Shipping News, who writes up the harbour arrivals.
explanation.definitionFit: In Annie Proulx's novel the hero Quoyle writes the column of vessel arrivals and departures for a Newfoundland paper.

clue.text: Detective hiding arm of a kind revealed in Elmore Leonard work

indicators.note: hiding means keeping something inside, so the detective holds the other pieces

parts.note: DI is Detective Inspector in British police ranks
a jib is the projecting arm of a crane
out means revealed or made public, as a secret that is out

explanation.surface: A sleuth conceals some weapon that is uncovered in a crime novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hiding' signals the container. 'arm' suggests a weapon, but it is a crane's arm. Djibouti (2010) is one of Leonard's last novels, about Somali pirates.
explanation.definitionFit: Djibouti is a 2010 thriller by Elmore Leonard, named after the African port where much of it is set.

clue.text: Where Ellis Hock lives with old lady and canon near India

parts.note: ma is a familiar word for one's mother, the old lady
a canon is a rule or law, as in church law
I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A person's home is with their mother and a churchman close to India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'canon' looks like a clergyman next to 'old lady', but it is a rule. Ellis Hock is a character in a work set in this African country.
explanation.definitionFit: The character Ellis Hock is placed in this landlocked southern African country in the work that features him.

clue.text: Is it possible in the future to get Talos's fee for naval correspondent?

parts.note: will marks the future tense, as in I will go
Talos is the setter, so Talos's (Talos is) becomes I am from the setter's point of view
a price is a fee or charge

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the setter will be paid in time for a letter from a sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading the pieces as a question gives 'Will I am price?' to match 'Is it possible'. William Price is Fanny's midshipman brother in Mansfield Park, who writes to her from sea.
explanation.definitionFit: In Jane Austen's Mansfield Park William Price serves in the navy and keeps up letters with his sister Fanny.

clue.text: Crime writer from Cardiff?

definitions.meaning: Irvine ... wrote the novel Crime as well as Trainspotting
a person or thing from Cardiff belongs to Wales; the question mark flags that a city stands for the whole country

explanation.surface: An author of detective fiction from the Welsh capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crime writer' reads as a genre, but Crime (2008) is a title by the Scottish novelist Irvine Welsh.
explanation.definitionFit: Irvine Welsh wrote Crime, and the adjective also describes anything from Wales, whose capital is Cardiff.

clue.text: He and I hare up rock to find unctuous bloke

indicators.note: rock means shake or sway, so the letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: Two people run up a rocky outcrop to find a greasy fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rock' rearranges HE and I HARE UP. Fittingly, the answer is also the name of a British rock band; it is the fawning clerk of Dickens's David Copperfield.
explanation.definitionFit: The clerk in David Copperfield is the classic oily, falsely humble flatterer, always claiming to be 'umble.

clue.text: Public statement of puritan gloom in the works

indicators.note: in the works means being processed or put together, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A declaration of Puritan dreariness is being prepared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the works' rearranges PURITAN GLOOM.
explanation.definitionFit: Proclaiming a law or decree formally to the people is a public announcement of it.

clue.text: One who thought Rialto set foolish

indicators.note: foolish means silly or muddled, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A clever person thought the Venetian bridge crowd were idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foolish' rearranges RIALTO SET.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek philosopher is the thinker par excellence, so he is fairly described as a man who thought.

clue.text: She delivered Patience Sparhawk to Tehran after revolution

indicators.note: after revolution means once turned around and overthrown, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman carried a patient to Iran's capital in the wake of the uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after revolution' rearranges TO TEHRAN. 'Delivered' sounds like a midwife, but Gertrude Atherton wrote the novel Patience Sparhawk and Her Times (1897).
explanation.definitionFit: The American novelist Gertrude Atherton produced the book Patience Sparhawk, so she brought it into the world.

clue.text: Fat fellow seen with rod on far side of river

indicators.note: on far side of means the rod comes after the river, beyond it

parts.note: the Fal is a river in Cornwall
a staff is a rod or stick

explanation.surface: A large man is spotted holding a fishing rod across the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on far side of' sets the rod after the river, which is in Cornwall, England. 'rod' and 'river' together paint an angler, but no fishing is involved.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Falstaff is Shakespeare's famously corpulent knight in the Henry IV plays and The Merry Wives of Windsor.

clue.text: "— is not England. Our ways are not your ways, and there shall be to you many strange things." (Bram Stoker)

definitions.text: "— is not England. Our ways are not your ways, and there shall be to you many strange things." (Bram Stoker)

parts.words: "— is not England. Our ways are not your ways, and there shall be to you many strange things." (Bram Stoker)
parts.note: a quotation clue: the Count in Dracula tells Jonathan Harker that his homeland is unlike England, and the blank names that region

explanation.surface: A line from Dracula with its opening place-name blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: In Stoker's novel the Count says this to Harker on his arrival at the castle, naming the region of Romania where he lives.
explanation.definitionFit: Count Dracula's home is this region in the Carpathians of Romania, which he contrasts with Harker's England.

clue.text: Greek character breaks school pact made before union

indicators.note: breaks means splits apart, with the letter placed in the gap

parts.note: a prep is a preparatory school
nu is the thirteenth letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A Greek student disrupts a school agreement signed before joining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaks' signals the container; 'union' here means marriage, not a trade union.
explanation.definitionFit: A prenuptial agreement is a contract a couple sign before marrying, settling money matters in advance.

clue.text: Royal murdered a French catholic held by daring type

indicators.note: held by means kept inside, so the daring type wraps round the other pieces

parts.note: Dan Dare is the space-hero of the British Eagle comic, a daring type
un is the French for a

explanation.surface: A bold person keeps hold of a French Catholic royal who was killed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held by' signals the container. Dan Dare is the 1950s British comic space hero. Duncan is the king Macbeth kills.
explanation.definitionFit: King Duncan of Scotland is stabbed in his sleep by Macbeth in Shakespeare's tragedy.

clue.text: A&E patches up area where 17 got smashed

indicators.note: up here means disturbed or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Hospital casualty staff patch up a district where a drunk came to grief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' rearranges A&E PATCHES. 17 is FALSTAFF, who drinks at the Boar's Head tavern in this street in the City of London; 'smashed' means drunk, not injured.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare places Falstaff's drinking at the Boar's Head inn in this old London street.

clue.text: Account of an addict cutting cocaine with heroin

indicators.note: cutting a drug means mixing it, so the letter goes into the middle of the word

parts.note: coke is slang for cocaine
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A tale of drug use, with cocaine adulterated using heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutting' puts H inside COKE: dealers 'cut' drugs by mixing in other substances. Chuck Palahniuk's novel Choke follows a sex addict.
explanation.definitionFit: Chuck Palahniuk's novel follows Victor Mancini, a sex addict, so the book is a story of one.

clue.text: Estonian city, one like Nancy with university

parts.note: Nancy in Oliver Twist is a prostitute, a woman sometimes called a tart

explanation.surface: A town in Estonia has a woman like Nancy at its college.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy is the streetwalker in Dickens's Oliver Twist, not the French city of Nancy that the place-name context suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Tartu is the second city of Estonia, home of the country's oldest university.

clue.text: Milliner's party gear is two varieties of dope

parts.note: tea is old slang for marijuana, one kind of dope
pot is slang for cannabis, a second kind of dope

explanation.surface: A hat-maker's celebration involves two sorts of drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The milliner is the Mad Hatter of Alice in Wonderland, whose tea party features this vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mad Hatter's tea party needs a vessel for brewing and pouring, the essential kit of such a gathering.

clue.text: Short extract from enlivening thing like Paradise Lost?

indicators.note: short means cut off at the end, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: to milk is to extract from, as in milking someone for money
a tonic is something that refreshes or enlivens

explanation.surface: A brief passage from something lively, resembling the epic poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' drops the last letter of MILK. 'extract' poses as a noun (a passage) but is the verb milk.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise Lost is the epic of John Milton, so the adjective describes something in his style.

clue.text: Some outspoken if federalist emitted a bad smell

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A blunt-talking federalist politician gave off an unpleasant odour.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'outspoken if federalist'. Niff is British slang for a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Niff is informal British for a stink, so as a past-tense verb it means gave off a nasty smell.

clue.text: Old man cracking safe with northern flyboy?

indicators.note: cracking here means the old man is working on the safe, placed right up against it

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
pa is a familiar word for father, one's old man

explanation.surface: A veteran burglar breaks open a safe with a northern accomplice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peter' is thieves' slang for a safe; 'cracking' sets PA right beside it. The flying boy of J. M. Barrie's play never grows up.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Barrie's boy hero flies to Neverland, so with the question mark he is literally a flying lad.
